nameStory: The 'common eastern' part of this bee's name tells you exactly what you need to know - it's the bumble bee you're most likely to encounter throughout eastern North America. The scientific name 'impatiens' means 'impatient,' possibly referring to their energetic, bustling behavior as they rapidly move from flower to flower. With over 42,000 observations in New England alone, this truly lives up to its 'common' reputation!
description: The Common Eastern Bumble Bee is a robust, fuzzy bee that's become the poster child for bumble bees across eastern North America. These social bees are excellent pollinators with their characteristic round, furry bodies covered in dense hair that helps them collect pollen. They're medium to large-sized bees, typically about the size of your thumb from tip to first knuckle. Their amazing adaptability allows them to thrive everywhere from wild meadows to city gardens, making them one of our most important native pollinators.

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Look for a mostly black bee with a bright yellow band across the front of the thorax (the fuzzy middle section behind the head), and usually another yellow band on the front part of the abdomen. The rest of the body is typically black, creating a distinctive yellow-on-black pattern.

idTips.label: Fuzzy Texture
idTips.description: The entire body is covered in dense, soft hair that looks almost plush - like a tiny flying teddy bear. This fuzz is so thick you can actually see individual hairs sticking out, especially when backlit by sunlight.

idTips.label: Flight Style
idTips.description: They fly with an audible buzz that's deeper and more continuous than a honey bee's hum. Their flight appears slightly clumsy or wobbly, as if they're too heavy for their wings, but they're actually quite agile.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly round and robust compared to other bees, with a noticeably fuzzy, barrel-shaped abdomen. They look substantial and well-fed, quite different from the more streamlined appearance of honey bees.

idTips.label: Foraging Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen 'buzz pollinating' - grabbing onto a flower and vibrating their flight muscles to shake pollen loose, creating an intense buzzing sound. They're particularly fond of tomato, blueberry, and eggplant flowers.

habitat: You'll find Common Eastern Bumble Bees just about everywhere in New England - they're incredibly adaptable! They thrive in gardens, meadows, forest edges, parks, and even busy urban areas with flowering plants. Look for them in areas with diverse flowering plants from spring through fall, from sea level to mountain elevations, and they're especially common around vegetable gardens, berry patches, and wildflower meadows.

seasonality.spring: Queens emerge from winter hibernation in early spring and can be seen searching for nesting sites, often appearing larger than workers you'll see later. They're among the first bees active, visiting early flowers like crocuses and fruit tree blossoms.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity with full colonies bustling about. You'll see smaller worker bees constantly visiting flowers, and this is the best time to observe their buzz pollination behavior on garden vegetables and wildflowers.
seasonality.fall: New queens and males emerge for mating flights, so you might see larger individuals again. Workers continue foraging on late-season flowers like asters and goldenrod until the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: Only the mated queens survive winter, hibernating in protected spots like under logs or leaf litter. No bumble bee activity is visible during the coldest months.

funFact: Common Eastern Bumble Bees are essentially living heating pads - they can 'shiver' their flight muscles to warm up their bodies to 95°F even when the air temperature is near freezing, allowing them to fly and forage in weather that would ground other bees!
confusionNotes: With 16 different bumble bee species in New England, identification can be tricky! The Common Eastern's mostly black body with yellow bands distinguishes it from species like the Tricolored Bumble Bee (which has white patches) or the Brown-belted Bumble Bee (which has brown coloring). Remember: if it's a bumble bee you're seeing frequently in your garden or local park, it's probably this common species.
contextualKnowledge: This species has become so valuable for commercial greenhouse pollination that they're now raised in captivity and shipped worldwide, which has helped spread them beyond their original range. Some bumble bee experts worry this commercial use might impact wild populations, making accurate identification of wild bees increasingly important for conservation monitoring.
compareHints: Among New England's bumble bees, the Common Eastern Bumble Bee is distinguished by its predominantly black coloration with limited yellow banding, unlike the Brown-belted Bumble Bee which has brown fur, or the Tricolored Bumble Bee which sports distinctive white patches. The Yellow-banded Bumble Bee has more extensive yellow coloring, while the Half-black Bumble Bee has a completely yellow abdomen. When in doubt, remember that the Common Eastern is aptly named - it's the one you're most likely to see!

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bumble bees, the Brown-belted is most similar to the Red-belted Bumble Bee, but has a duller, more brownish belt versus bright rusty-red.
Among New England's many bumble bee species, the Two-spotted stands out for its clean black and yellow pattern with those diagnostic two spots.
The orange band is what sets the Tricolored Bumble Bee apart from its many relatives in New England.
Compared to the Common Eastern Bumble Bee, the Perplexing Bumble Bee has more white hairs on the head and distinctive reddish mandible tips.
Unlike the Common Eastern Bumble Bee which has more irregular yellow patches, the Yellow-banded has clean, complete yellow bands.

Northern Amber Bumble Bees stand out from other New England bumble bees by their uniform golden-yellow body combined with contrasting pale head hairs—most other species have distinct color bands or patterns.
Compared to the Common Eastern Bumble Bee, Half-black Bumble Bees are noticeably smaller and have more defined black banding rather than the Common Eastern's more blended yellow and black pattern.

Among New England's bumble bees, the Golden Northern stands out for its uniform golden-yellow coloration, while most relatives like the Common Eastern Bumble Bee have distinct black and white/yellow banding patterns.
Unlike social bumble bees in its genus, the Lemon Cuckoo Bumble Bee lacks pollen baskets (specialized hairs for carrying pollen) since it doesn't need to provision its own nest.
Unlike other cuckoo bumble bees in New England like the Lemon Cuckoo Bumble Bee, the Yellowish Cuckoo has more muted, golden-yellow tones rather than bright lemon-yellow.
Red-belted bumble bees are much smaller than common eastern bumble bees and lack the solid yellow thorax of many other species.
